descriptive_title: Grade 2 Mathematics: Numbers — Reading, Composing, Comparing, Estimating, and Fair-Sharing Numbers to 200, plus Even/Odd and Halves/Thirds/Sixths (B1.1–B1.7)
subject: Mathematics

curriculum_expectations.B1.1: read, represent, compose, and decompose whole numbers up to and including 200, using a variety of tools and strategies, and describe various ways they are used in everyday life
curriculum_expectations.B1.2: compare and order whole numbers up to and including 200, in various contexts
curriculum_expectations.B1.3: estimate the number of objects in collections of up to 200 and verify their estimates by counting
curriculum_expectations.B1.4: count to 200, including by 20s, 25s, and 50s, using a variety of tools and strategies
curriculum_expectations.B1.5: describe what makes a number even or odd
curriculum_expectations.B1.6: use drawings to represent, solve, and compare the results of fair-share problems that involve sharing up to 10 items among 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 10 sharers
curriculum_expectations.B1.7: recognize that one third and two sixths of the same whole are equal, in fair-sharing contexts

unit_overview: A 5-day Grade 2 unit on Numbers framed around the 'Place Value Detective Agency' — Detective Hugo Hundreds (a sharp-eyed sleuth with a 'HUNDREDS' top hat), Detective Tina Tens (his energetic partner with a magnifying glass), and Detective Ona Ones (the tiny but mighty rookie). Day 1 'Hundreds Hideouts' opens the agency and introduces three-digit place value with base-ten blocks, plus skip-counting by 20s, 25s, and 50s on a 0-200 number line (B1.1, B1.4). Day 2 'Compose, Decompose, Compare' is the keystone for B1.1 + B1.2: children break apart and rebuild numbers to 200 in flexible ways and compare same-hundreds and different-hundreds numbers using place-value reasoning. Day 3 'The Even/Odd Investigation' tackles B1.5 with the pair-up test (can you make pairs?) and connects to skip-counting by 2s as the 'even number generator' (B1.4 reinforced). Day 4 'Estimation Stake-Out' uses the chunk-of-10 → chunk-of-100 strategy lift from Grade 1 to estimate collections of up to 200 (B1.3). Day 5 'Fair Shares with Thirds and Sixths' is the capstone: fair-sharing collections of 6, 9, and 12 between 2/3/4/6 sharers (B1.6) and the third-on-sixths reveal showing 1/3 = 2/6 (B1.7). The unit progresses concrete (real base-ten blocks, hundreds chart, paper cookies) → representational (place-value mats, number-line jumps, fraction circles) → abstract (numerical comparison, fraction notation, equation writing).
unit_learning_goal: Children will read, represent, compose, decompose, compare, order, estimate, and count whole numbers to 200; describe what makes a number even or odd; share collections fairly between 2-10 sharers; and recognise that one third equals two sixths of the same whole.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Numbers to 200 are made of hundreds, tens, and ones. We can count to 200 by 20s, 25s, and 50s.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can read and represent numbers to 200 with base-ten blocks and count to 200 by 20s, 25s, and 50s.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Detective Hugo introduces the Place Value Detective Agency; whole-class base-ten block builds for numbers 100-200; 0-200 number line skip-counting by 20s, 25s, 50s.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Numbers can be split apart and rebuilt in many ways. To compare numbers, look at the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can compose and decompose numbers to 200 in different ways, and compare numbers using place-value reasoning.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Decomposition mats with multiple flexible splits (e.g., 147 = 100+40+7 = 130+17 = 50+97); compare-the-jar with same-hundreds pairs (147 vs 174) and different-hundreds pairs (89 vs 102).

lesson_arc.big_idea: Even numbers can pair up with no leftover. Odd numbers always have one left over. Counting by 2s only lands on even numbers.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can describe what makes a number even or odd, and use the pair-up test to check.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Pair-up test with cubes for numbers 1-30; even/odd sort with 100 sticky notes 1-100; connection between skip-counting by 2s and the even numbers.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Smart estimates use a chunk strategy. For collections to 200, we chunk by 10 first then count the chunks, or chunk by 100 if the collection is huge.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can estimate the number of objects in a collection up to 200 using a chunk strategy and verify by counting.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Detective Tina's chunk-strategy upgrade — from chunk-of-10 (Grade 1) to chunk-of-100 for big collections; estimation jars at three scales (50, 100, 175) with the per-pair verification routine.

lesson_arc.lesson_title: Fair Shares with Thirds and Sixths
lesson_arc.big_idea: Sharing fairly between 3 friends gives thirds. Between 6 friends gives sixths. One third equals two sixths of the same thing.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can share a small collection fairly between 2, 3, 4, or 6 friends, and tell that one third equals two sixths.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Fair-share rounds with 6, 9, and 12 cookies between 2/3/4/6 sharers; the pizza-overlay reveal showing 1/3 = 2/6; fraction-strip comparison of unit fractions 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8.

recurring_characters.name: Detective Hugo Hundreds
recurring_characters.role: Lead character of the Place Value Detective Agency. Anchors Lesson 1 and reappears throughout. Loves big numbers and place-value mysteries. Catchphrase: 'Look at the hundreds first!'
recurring_characters.visual_description: A clever-looking detective with a tall top hat marked 'HUNDREDS' (with a small '100' badge). Wears a long brown coat with magnifying glass in the pocket, sharp eyes, friendly smile. Carries a notebook for recording case findings.

recurring_characters.name: Detective Tina Tens
recurring_characters.role: Hugo's partner. Anchors the place-value composition work in Lesson 2 and the estimation work in Lesson 4. Specialises in the 'tens' part of the number — counting by 10s and 20s.
recurring_characters.visual_description: An energetic detective wearing a striped vest with '10' patches, a cap, and holding a magnifying glass. Eager expression, slightly shorter than Hugo. Often jotting numbers in a small detective pad.

recurring_characters.name: Detective Ona Ones
recurring_characters.role: The tiny but mighty rookie detective. Anchors the even/odd investigation in Lesson 3. Specialises in the 'ones' place — checking which numbers can pair up and which always have one leftover.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A small detective with a single '1' badge on her shirt and a tiny bowtie. Holds a paper-clip 'evidence bag' for collecting one-by-one items. Determined expression.

threaded_vocabulary.child_friendly_definition: What a digit is worth depending on where it sits. In 147, the 1 is worth 100, the 4 is worth 40, and the 7 is worth 7.
Groups of 100. In 147, there is 1 hundred.
Groups of 10. In 147, there are 4 tens (which is 40).
Single units. In 147, there are 7 ones.
Put parts together to make a number. 100 + 40 + 7 composes 147.
Split a number into parts. 147 decomposes to 100 + 40 + 7 (or 130 + 17, or many others).
A number that can pair up with no leftover. 8 is even because 4 pairs of 2 fit perfectly.
A number that always has one leftover when you try to pair up. 9 is odd because 4 pairs and 1 left over.
One of three equal parts of a whole. If 3 friends share a pizza fairly, each gets one third.
One of six equal parts of a whole. If 6 friends share a pizza fairly, each gets one sixth.

manipulatives_index.name: Base-Ten Blocks
manipulatives_index.description: Per-pair set: 4 hundred-flats + 20 ten-rods + 30 unit-cubes. Used for Lesson 1 representation, Lesson 2 composition.

manipulatives_index.name: Place-Value Mat
manipulatives_index.description: Letter-size mat with three labeled columns: HUNDREDS, TENS, ONES. Used in Lessons 1 and 2 for organising base-ten representations.

manipulatives_index.name: 0-200 Number Line
manipulatives_index.description: Long printable strip showing numbers 0 to 200 with cells ~2.5in each. Used in Lesson 1 for skip-counting and Lesson 2 for ordering.

manipulatives_index.name: Number Decomposition Cards
manipulatives_index.description: Set of 30 cards. Each shows a target number (47, 89, 132, 178, etc.) and three blank slots for the child to write three different decompositions.

manipulatives_index.name: Compare-Two-Numbers Cards
manipulatives_index.description: Set of 24 number-pair cards (e.g., 147 vs 174, 89 vs 102, 134 vs 143). Used in Lesson 2 partner game.

manipulatives_index.name: Pair-Up Cubes
manipulatives_index.description: Per-pair set of 30 connecting cubes. Used in Lesson 3 even/odd investigation — children try to pair up the cubes.

manipulatives_index.name: Hundreds Chart 1-100
manipulatives_index.description: Letter-size hundreds chart used in Lesson 3 for the even/odd sort and Lesson 1 skip-counting reference.

manipulatives_index.name: Estimation Jars
manipulatives_index.description: Three clear jars of different sizes for Lesson 4 estimation: small (~50 items), medium (~100 items), large (~175 items). Items can be buttons, marbles, beans, or cubes.

manipulatives_index.name: Third/Sixth Pizza Cards
manipulatives_index.description: Printable letter-size cards showing whole pizzas, thirds, and sixths. Used in Lesson 5 to reveal that 1/3 = 2/6 visually.

manipulatives_index.name: Sharing Paper Plates
manipulatives_index.description: Set of 6 paper plates per group. Children deal collections fairly between 2, 3, 4, or 6 sharers in Lesson 5.

materials_overview: Base-Ten Blocks: ~4 hundred-flats + 20 tens + 30 ones per pair (or one classroom set)
0-200 Number Line: one classroom strip (assembled from 11 letter pages)
Number Decomposition Cards: 30 cards per class
Estimation Jars: three clear glass jars (small, medium, large)
Third/Sixth Pizza Cards: one set per group
Sharing Paper Plates: 6 per group of 4 children
Anchor chart 'Hundreds, Tens, Ones' with example representations
Sticky notes 1-100 (for the Lesson 3 even/odd sort)

assessment_strategy.diagnostic: Lesson 1 place-value snapshot: each child reads three numbers (47, 132, 189) and represents them with base-ten blocks. Tally per-child accuracy on (a) reading the numeral, (b) building with the correct number of hundreds-tens-ones, and (c) counting the total of the build. Children who struggle with reading 132 vs 312 (digit-order confusion) need explicit place-value reteach during Lesson 2.
assessment_strategy.formative: Lesson 2 decomposition tracker: per-child evidence on whether the child can produce 3+ different decompositions for a given number (e.g., 147 = 100+40+7 = 130+17 = 50+97). Lesson 3 even/odd tracker: can the child explain WHY a number is even or odd (pair-up test)? Lesson 4 estimation tracker: does the child use a chunk strategy and explain it?
assessment_strategy.summative: Lesson 5 Fair-Share + Fraction Equivalence worksheet — three priced share scenarios (with sharers including 2, 3, 4, 6) + the 1/3 = 2/6 equation prompt. Captures B1.6 and B1.7 explicitly. Combined with the formative trackers, the teacher has evidence for all 7 expectations B1.1-B1.7.

pedagogical_notes: B1.1 (numbers to 200) extends Grade 1's B1.2 (numbers to 50) by adding the HUNDREDS place. The most common misconception is digit-order confusion: children read 132 as 'one-three-two' or '132' but sometimes write 312 by mistake. The place-value mat is the explicit fix — labels HUNDREDS, TENS, ONES enforce position.

B1.2 (compare numbers to 200) requires the place-value rule: look at hundreds first, then tens, then ones. Children who default to ones-first reasoning (looking at the rightmost digit) get same-hundreds pairs wrong (147 vs 174 — they pick 147 because it has 7 ones).

B1.4 (count by 20s, 25s, 50s) is harder than Grade 1's count by 5s and 10s because the multiples are bigger and irregular. 25s are particularly tricky — 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175, 200 — children sometimes default to 25, 30, 35 (count-by-5s habit). The 0-200 number line is the embodied repair.

B1.5 (even/odd) is where Grade 2 introduces the pair-up rule explicitly. Children should be able to take a small collection and physically pair the items — leftover means odd. Connection to skip-counting by 2s reinforces: counting by 2s lands ONLY on even numbers.

B1.6 (fair-share with 2-10 sharers) extends Grade 1's B1.6 (2 and 4 sharers) by adding 3, 5, 6, 8 sharers. The harder cases are sharing 6 between 4 (1½ each) or 9 between 6 (1½ each) — half-shares from non-trivial dividends. Pre-cut paper cookies remain the canonical scaffold.

B1.7 (1/3 = 2/6) is the equivalence reveal — analogous to Grade 1's 1/2 = 2/4 but with thirds and sixths. The pizza-overlay demo (overlay one third on top of two sixths) is the visual proof. Children who saw 1/2 = 2/4 in Grade 1 generalise quickly; children new to fraction equivalence need the overlay step.
canadian_context_notes: Numbers up to 200 align with Canadian children's everyday experience: 167 hockey players in the league, 132 students in the school, 189 days of school per year. Canadian context puts numbers in places kids already see them.
Hundreds chart shows numbers 1-100 in a 10x10 grid — a Canadian classroom standard from K onward. Detective Hugo's notebook in the artwork can be visualised as a small Canadian-style spiral notebook.
Pizza fair-shares can swap to butter tarts (cut into thirds) or tourtière slices for cultural variation in Quebec or French-language classrooms.

Lesson 4 estimation jars can be filled with seasonal items: Halloween candy in October, hockey-puck stickers in November, Valentine's hearts in February — keeps the estimation task contextually fresh.
